subChunks.title: Capstone — Production-Grade Full-Stack React Application
subChunks.hookHtml: The Lead capstone is not a feature — it is an architecture. You have all the tools: Server Actions, streaming, observability, i18n, E2E tests, CI/CD, security hardening, PWA, performance optimisation, micro-frontend boundaries, a monorepo. The challenge is knowing which tools to use, which to defer, and which to deliberately leave out. Production-grade means: it handles failure gracefully, it's observable, it's secure, it ships reliably, and the next engineer can understand it without you.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The production checklist

// What 'production-grade' actually means:

✅ RELIABILITY
- Error boundaries at every async boundary
- Retry logic for transient failures (React Query's retry option)
- Graceful degradation when optional features fail
- Offline support for core read paths (PWA + NetworkFirst cache)

✅ OBSERVABILITY
- Sentry with user context, tags, and breadcrumbs
- Core Web Vitals reported to analytics
- Structured logging with correlation IDs
- Bundle size enforced in CI

✅ SECURITY
- No secrets in the frontend bundle
- HttpOnly cookies for auth tokens
- DOMPurify on all dangerouslySetInnerHTML usage
- Content Security Policy header
- npm audit in CI

✅ PERFORMANCE
- LCP < 2.5s on 4G mobile
- No render-blocking resources
- Route-based code splitting
- No render loops (verified with Profiler)

✅ ACCESSIBILITY
- WCAG 2.1 AA
- jest-axe in component tests
- Keyboard navigation for all interactive elements
- Focus management on route changes

✅ INTERNATIONALISATION
- No hardcoded strings (all through i18n)
- Pluralisation handled by i18next (not string concatenation)
- RTL layout tested for Arabic/Hebrew

✅ QUALITY
- TypeScript strict mode — zero any
- ESLint with react-hooks, jsx-a11y, no-explicit-any
- 80%+ test coverage on business logic
- Pre-commit hooks (lint-staged + Husky)

✅ DEPLOYMENT
- CI pipeline: lint → type-check → test → build → E2E → deploy
- Preview deployments on every PR
- Production deployment requires passing E2E suite
- Automated dependency updates (Dependabot)

Architecture decision for the capstone

// ADR-0001: Application Architecture
// Status: Accepted

// Decision: Next.js App Router (not Vite + React Router)
// Reason: The guild management platform has:
// - Public quest board (needs SSR for SEO)
// - Authenticated admin area (SPA behaviour fine)
// - API mutations (Server Actions eliminate separate API layer)
// - Streaming dashboard (App Router Suspense streaming)

// ADR-0002: State Management
// Server state: TanStack Query (not App Router cache alone)
// Reason: Admin area has complex optimistic updates and
// fine-grained invalidation patterns App Router cache doesn't support.
// Client state: Zustand for cross-component UI state.
// Local state: useState/useReducer.

// ADR-0003: Component Architecture
// Radix UI primitives + custom design tokens
// Reason: Accessibility is too complex to implement correctly;
// Radix solves it once. Our design system skins it.

// ADR-0004: Testing Strategy
// Unit: Vitest for utilities
// Component: Testing Library for components
// E2E: Playwright for critical paths only (login, quest acceptance, billing)

Putting it together: the request lifecycle

// What happens when a user accepts a quest in production:

// 1. Click → Server Action fires (no API round-trip)
// 2. useOptimistic updates UI immediately (perceived performance)
// 3. Server Action: Zod validates, DB mutates, cache revalidated
// 4. On success: TanStack Query invalidates quest list
// 5. On error: optimistic update reverts, error boundary catches
// 6. Sentry breadcrumb records the action with userId + questId
// 7. If offline: mutation queued in IndexedDB, replayed via background sync
// 8. E2E test verifies the full flow in CI on every PR

// The 8-step flow above involves:
// - React 19 (useOptimistic, Server Actions)
// - Next.js (revalidatePath)
// - TanStack Query (cache invalidation)
// - Zod (validation)
// - Sentry (observability)
// - PWA background sync (offline support)
// - Playwright (verification)
// Every tool justified; nothing added speculatively.

What a Lead engineer ships vs a Senior engineer

// Senior engineer ships:
// ✅ Correct, well-tested, performant code
// ✅ Good component abstractions
// ✅ Proper TypeScript

// Lead engineer additionally ships:
// ✅ Architecture that scales to the team's next 18 months
// ✅ Documented decisions (ADRs) that survive personnel changes
// ✅ CI pipeline that enforces quality without code review overhead
// ✅ Observability that means you know about problems before users report them
// ✅ Security posture that survives a dependency compromise
// ✅ Onboarding path: a new engineer is productive in 2 days, not 2 weeks

// The test: if you were hit by a bus tomorrow,
// could the team ship with confidence?
// That's what production-grade means.

Vex: "The most important word in 'production-grade' is 'grade' — it's a level of care, not a feature list. You can have all the tools and still ship a fragile system. The question is: have you applied each tool to the right problem, in the right place, with the right trade-offs understood? That judgment — not the tools — is what makes a Lead engineer."

storyBeats.text: Every tool learned. Every pattern understood. The question is no longer 'how do I implement this?' — it's 'should I implement this, and if so, where, and with what trade-offs?' That question has no syntax. It requires judgment. Judgment is earned through every bug fixed, every post-mortem read, every ADR written.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: You have all the tools. The Apprentice learned to render. The Junior learned to build. The Senior learned to build correctly and performantly. The Lead builds systems that other engineers can build on — systems that explain themselves, enforce their own standards, and degrade gracefully when things go wrong. That's the arc.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: The hardest skill is knowing what not to build. Not every app needs micro-frontends. Not every mutation needs optimistic updates. Not every component needs a state machine. Production-grade is the minimum viable architecture for your specific problem — no more, no less.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Architecture synthesis exercise — design the production system:

  • Write the ADR for your most important architectural decision in the quest board (state management, routing, or testing strategy) — include context, decision, consequences, and alternatives
  • Write the production checklist items that are most critical for the quest board specifically — justify each one
  • Sketch the complete request lifecycle for the quest acceptance flow — every layer it touches from click to database and back
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build and ship a production-grade guild management application. It must satisfy the full production checklist: (1) Next.js App Router with Server Actions, streaming Suspense, and Edge middleware for auth. (2) TanStack Query for server state with optimistic updates and error recovery. (3) Sentry observability with user context, breadcrumbs, and Core Web Vitals RUM. (4) i18n supporting English and one other language with correct pluralisation. (5) Playwright E2E suite covering login flow, quest acceptance, and error state — running in CI. (6) GitHub Actions pipeline: lint → type-check → test → E2E → deploy preview (PR) / production (main). (7) PWA with offline quest board viewing and background sync for acceptance mutations. (8) Security: HttpOnly auth cookies, DOMPurify, CSP header, npm audit clean. (9) ADRs for every major architectural decision. (10) CONTRIBUTING.md with standards, PR template, and onboarding guide. Deploy to a public URL and measure your Lighthouse scores.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between 'correct code' and 'production-grade code' — what dimensions of quality does production add beyond functional correctness? Walk through the complete request lifecycle for a user action in a production React application: what layers does it pass through, what can go wrong at each layer, and how does a well-architected application handle each failure mode? Reflect on the full React learning arc from Apprentice to Lead — what is the single most important concept at each tier, and how do they build on each other?

questions.prompt: A new senior engineer joins the team and says 'we should migrate to micro-frontends — it's the modern architecture.' What questions should you ask before agreeing?
options: What specific problem are we solving? What is the current pain point that micro-frontends would address? What is the migration cost? What new problems does it introduce (shared dependencies, cross-team coordination, deployment complexity)?
What framework does the engineer want to use for the shell?
How many teams are working on the codebase currently?
Whether the current application uses React or another framework
questions.answer: What specific problem are we solving? What is the current pain point that micro-frontends would address? What is the migration cost? What new problems does it introduce (shared dependencies, cross-team coordination, deployment complexity)?
questions.explanation: Architecture decisions should be driven by problems, not patterns. Micro-frontends solve specific problems: independent deployability across many teams, true technology diversity, organisational scaling. If none of those apply, micro-frontends add significant complexity (shared dependency management, integration testing, cross-MFE communication, build pipeline complexity) for no benefit. A Lead engineer evaluates every proposal against the actual constraints of the specific system.

questions.prompt: You're starting a new React project for an internal admin tool used by 10 employees on modern browsers. Which of these is the MOST production-grade choice?
options: Vite + React Router + TanStack Query + TypeScript strict — minimal stack that matches the actual requirements; no SSR (no SEO needed), no PWA (users are on desktops), no i18n (English-only company), no micro-frontends (one team)
Next.js App Router with micro-frontends, full i18n, PWA with offline support, and Module Federation
Create React App with Redux Toolkit — battle-tested and well-documented
Remix with SSR — always choose SSR for production applications
questions.answer: Vite + React Router + TanStack Query + TypeScript strict — minimal stack that matches the actual requirements; no SSR (no SEO needed), no PWA (users are on desktops), no i18n (English-only company), no micro-frontends (one team)
questions.explanation: Production-grade is not 'maximum tools' — it's 'minimum viable architecture for the actual requirements.' An internal admin tool has different requirements than a public consumer product. SSR adds complexity with no SEO benefit for an authenticated tool. Micro-frontends require multiple teams to justify their coordination overhead. PWA offline support is unnecessary if users are always in the office on fast connections. The production checklist still applies (TypeScript, testing, CI, observability, security) — but the architecture choices are shaped by the actual problem.
